summary: Defines a Uniform Resource Name namespace that lets Object Identifiers (the dotted numbers used to name things in ASN.1 and similar systems) be written as URNs. This gives those numbers a standard, location-independent text form. It was replaced by RFC 3061.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3001 defines how to write an Object Identifier as a URN using the urn:oid: prefix. It carries over the OID rules for uniqueness and persistence, but does not define a way to look up an identifier.

questions: how to write an object identifier as a urn
how to write oid as urn
subtitle: A URN format for expressing Object Identifiers as URIs.

tldr.problem: Object Identifiers needed a standard way to be expressed as URIs while keeping their existing assignment and persistence rules.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the oid URN namespace, with an identifier body made of dot-separated digits following the cited string encoding rules.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3001 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 3061.

today: RFC 3001 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 3061.

sections.title: Object Identifiers
sections.content:
An Object Identifier (OID) is a series of digits separated by delimiters. Once an entity receives an OID, it can assign new OIDs beneath it. Examples in the memo include 1.3.6.1 and 1.3.6.1.4.1.

The RFC defines a formal URN namespace named oid for encoding an ASN.1 Object Identifier as a URI. The leading assigned branches described here are 0 for ITU-T, 1 for ISO, and 2 for joint ISO/ITU-T assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: An OID is a name written as a sequence of numbers. The RFC gives OIDs a standard URN form so they can be written as URIs.

sections.title: The oid URN Form
sections.content:
The namespace identifier is oid. The part after it follows the string rules cited from RFC 1778: digits are separated by periods, with the most significant digit at the left and the least significant at the right. For example, the OID 1.3.6.1 is written as urn:oid:1.3.6.1.

OID assignment rules require each identifier to be unique and not reassigned or reused. The URN namespace inherits those uniqueness and persistence rules by reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Write urn:oid: before the OID's dot-separated digits. The identifier keeps its OID rules: it must be unique and cannot be reused.

sections.title: Resolution, Matching, and Security
sections.content:
The memo defines no resolution mechanism and no validation mechanism for these URNs. It says lexical equivalence is determined by an exact string match, and the namespace has global scope.

The security section adds no security considerations beyond those inherent in using unverifiable OIDs. The examples show the URN form for several OIDs, including the Internet OID and an OID used for private MIBs.
sections.plainLanguage: This format gives OIDs a standard written form, but the RFC does not define a service for looking them up or checking them. Matching uses an exact string comparison.

references.text: Howes, T., Kille, S., Yeong, W., and C. Robbins, "The String Representation of Standard Attribute Syntaxes", RFC 1778, March 1995.
